strengths: Clear problem identification: The paper effectively motivates two concrete limitations of existing KD methods (softmax smoothing and DLD's solution space restriction) with compelling examples (Figure 1)

Sound theoretical contributions: Proposition 1, Theorem 2, and Theorem 3 are rigorously proven and provide theoretical guarantees. Theorem 2 particularly establishes that CSD's solution set properly contains DLD's, addressing logit shift invariance
Efficient gradient computation: Theorem 3's reduction from O(|V|²) objective to O(|V|) gradient via clever factorization w(y,x)=w₁(y)w₂(x) is non-trivial and practically valuable

Comprehensive experimental evaluation: Multiple benchmarks (5 instruction-following + 3 task-specific), model scales (0.1B-7B), 10+ baselines, multiple metrics (ROUGE-L, Self-BLEU, Distinct-N, GPT-4), and ablations strengthen claims

Design space exploration: The parameterization by (w₁, w₂) enabling mode-seeking/mode-covering variants is elegant, and Figure 3a shows CSD enveloping the diversity-fidelity frontier of existing methods
Consistent improvements: CSD shows improvements across all evaluated settings and works orthogonally with on-policy methods (Table 2), suggesting broad applicability
Practical algorithm with clear implementation: Algorithm 1 and Code 1 provide implementable solutions, addressing the training instability problem through well-motivated logarithmic transformation
weaknesses: Modest empirical improvements with fairness concerns: Average improvement 20.65 (CSD) vs 20.00 (SRKL) in Table 1 is 0.65 ROUGE-L points with overlapping error bars. Critical fairness issue: OpenLLaMA experiments fix CSD's learning rate to 1e-4 without tuning while baselines use official settings. Task-specific distillation shows validation loss unavailable for CSD, affecting checkpoint selection fairness

Incremental conceptual novelty: Core contribution adapts existing concrete score matching (Meng et al. 2022) to autoregressive LLMs. While solving practical issues, the conceptual novelty is moderate. Logarithmic transformation for training stability is straightforward

Theory-practice gap: Theorems assume 'sufficient model capacity' without quantification. No analysis of why/when the larger solution set helps under limited capacity (the practical scenario). Empirical validation (Figure 8) limited to one setting. No convergence analysis or sample complexity bounds

Unexplained baseline failures: Table 3 shows TV/SKL/SRKL achieve 0% accuracy on GSM8K versus 25.78% for CSD, but lacks mechanistic analysis. Receives only speculation about 'mode-seeking tendencies.' Case studies (Tables 7-10) are superficial

Limited ablation studies: Only T/U/S weighting choices evaluated in Table 4. Monte Carlo comparison (Figure 5) only for (S,S). No systematic sensitivity analysis across tasks. Restrictive factorization assumption w(y,x)=w₁(y)w₂(x) not justified

Limited scope and scalability: Maximum model size 7B (relatively small). No evaluation on 13B/70B models. No multilingual evaluation. No actual wall-clock time comparisons despite efficiency claims. O(|V|) gradient complexity still involves 50K+ vocabulary operations

Experimental concerns affecting confidence: OpenLLaMA results potentially biased by inconsistent hyperparameter tuning. Task-specific checkpoint selection differs between CSD and baselines. Only 5 random seeds for main results

Incomplete theoretical justification: 'Sufficient capacity' assumption undefined quantitatively. No degradation analysis when capacity insufficient. Weighting factorization lacks theoretical motivation beyond enabling efficiency

strengths: Clear problem motivation with effective visualizations (Figure 1) illustrating softmax smoothing and logit shift invariance limitations
Solid theoretical contributions: Proposition 1 (consistency), Theorem 2 (solution superset), and Theorem 3 (efficient O(|V|) gradient computation) with sound proofs
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple tasks, model families (GPT-2, OpenLLaMA, GEMMA), and diverse metrics (ROUGE-L, Self-BLEU, Distinct-N, GPT-4 feedback)
Extensive comparisons with 10+ baseline loss functions and thorough ablation studies on weighting function choices
Practical implementation with efficient gradient computation and provided code for reproducibility
weaknesses: Limited novelty: primarily adapts concrete score matching (Meng et al., 2022) from discrete diffusion models; the main innovation (taking logarithms for stability) is a straightforward engineering solution rather than a fundamental methodological advance

Marginal empirical improvements: 0.87 ROUGE-L point over best baseline (20.65 vs 19.78), and only 0.26 points over DLD (S) when controlling for weighting, which may not justify additional hyperparameter complexity

Incomplete comparison with most relevant baseline: DLD appears only in ablations (Table 4), not in main results (Table 1); direct comparison critical to validate key claims about solution space advantages
Theoretical solution set advantage does not clearly translate to practice: with sufficient capacity and training, DLD should learn relative logit differences; the practical gap remains unclear

Weighting function design lacks principled guidance: factorization w(yt,x)=w₁(yt)w₂(x) not justified; only three choices tested (T,U,S); task-specific experiments require (T,S) for math due to mode collapse with other choices, indicating hyperparameter sensitivity without clear selection methodology
Experimental confounds weaken loss-only claims: Table 2 mixes dataset strategies (Fix, Ada, On) across methods; unclear how much improvement comes from loss vs. on-policy data composition
The contribution is framed as 'Concrete Score Distillation' but reduces to weighted logit MSE (Eq. 8); connection to concrete score matching theory feels post-hoc
No wall-clock time comparisons despite O(|V|) claim; constant factors in Algorithm 1 (weighted sums over full vocabulary) could be substantial
Task-specific instability: multiple baselines achieve 0% accuracy on GSM8K; CSD requires switching to (T,S) weighting, contradicting claims of generality

Insufficient analysis of why CSD works: what drives improvement—logit-level matching, flexible weighting, or broader solution set? The token-dependent residual constants shown in Figure 8 lack performance impact analysis

strengths: Well-motivated problem identification with clear articulation of logit shift invariance limitations in prior work
Solid theoretical foundation grounded in score matching with three rigorous results: consistency (Prop. 1), solution superset (Theorem 2), and efficient O(|V|) gradient computation (Theorem 3)
Exceptionally comprehensive experiments across 8 distinct settings with multiple model scales, 10+ baselines, and thorough ablations demonstrating consistent improvements
Elegant technical solution resolving training instability and computational complexity of discrete score matching for autoregressive LLMs
Clean mathematical formulation with implementation details provided (Algorithm 1, Code 1) supporting reproducibility
Flexible design space enabling both mode-seeking and mode-covering variants with evidence of improved fidelity-diversity trade-offs
weaknesses: Marginal empirical improvements undermine practical significance: Table 1 average gain of 0.65 points (20.65 vs. 20.00) with many individual benchmarks showing overlapping confidence intervals (e.g., Dolly: 24.94±0.29 vs. 24.53±0.21)

Key theoretical insight (logit shift invariance solution superset) shows limited practical impact: Figure 8 demonstrates CSD learns token-dependent constants but performance improvement over DLD is modest (20.65 vs. 20.39)
Incomplete baseline comparisons: SKL and AB acknowledged to underperform due to missing components (pretraining losses, on-policy training), compromising 'loss-level comparison' fairness in Table 1
Insufficient guidance for practitioners on weighting function selection despite large performance variations (5.91 to 20.65 across w1,w2 choices in Table 4)
Unexplained catastrophic failures: TV, SKL, SRKL achieve 0% accuracy on GSM8K (Table 3) with only speculative attribution to mode-seeking; root cause analysis absent
Missing critical analysis: no wall-clock training time comparisons; limited investigation of which task/model characteristics favor CSD; absent sensitivity analysis for large vocabulary sizes (200K+)

Presentation could be clearer: abrupt transition from concrete score (Eq. 6) to CSD (Eq. 7-8); Algorithm 1 notation is dense; scope limited to autoregressive models without discussion of other architectures

strengths: Clear problem motivation: Figure 1 effectively demonstrates how softmax smoothing and DLD's solution set restrictions limit existing approaches
Solid theoretical contributions: Proposition 1 establishes consistency, Theorem 2 rigorously shows the broader solution set of CSD, and Theorem 3 provides efficient O(|V|) gradient computation
Comprehensive experimental validation across diverse settings (task-agnostic, task-specific, general chat) with multiple teacher-student pairs and 10+ baselines
Thorough ablation studies examining weighting functions, fidelity-diversity trade-offs, temperature scaling, calibration, and gradient computation methods
Practical design with clean algorithms (Algorithm 1), reference code, and demonstrated orthogonal integration with on-policy methods (Table 2)
Rich analysis with insightful visualizations (Figures 9-13) showing solution set exploration and logit offset dynamics supporting theoretical claims
weaknesses: Modest empirical improvements: Gains are often 1-2% over baselines (e.g., 20.65 vs 20.00 SRKL in Table 1; 7.42 vs 7.28 MT-Bench in Table 4) with no statistical significance testing to validate claims of consistent superiority

Experimental fairness concerns: Baselines (SKL, AB) underperform compared to original papers; CSD uses fixed learning rate (1e-4) while baselines use original settings; raises questions about equal hyperparameter tuning

Limited theoretical analysis: Theorem 2 proves Θ*_CSD ⊃ Θ*_DLD but lacks analysis of why larger solution sets improve generalization; connection between logit shift invariance and better performance is only empirically demonstrated

Arbitrary weighting function design: Default choice of 'detached student probability' lacks clear justification; limited guidance for practitioners on choosing w1, w2 for new tasks; adaptive weighting (Section D.2) appears ad-hoc

Incremental novelty: Concrete score matching is from Meng et al. (2022); main contributions are addressing instability via log transformation and efficient gradient computation—solid engineering but limited conceptual novelty

Limited experimental scope: Largest student model is 3B (from 7B teacher); no evaluation on larger students, non-standard architectures (MoE, sparse), or specialized domains; missing comparisons with recent work (e.g., speculative distillation cited but not compared)

Computational cost not clearly advantageous: Table 9 shows training time sometimes higher than baselines (26.64s vs 25.84s for KL); no discussion of scalability to massive vocabularies (256k) or per-token overhead
Incomplete failure mode analysis: Table 3 shows DLD at 0% accuracy on GSM8K with only speculative explanation about mode-seeking; deeper investigation of when/why CSD excels would strengthen claims

strengths: Clear problem identification: Well-articulated limitations of softmax smoothing and DLD's restriction on solution space
Solid theoretical contributions: Proposition 1 (consistency), Theorem 2 (solution superset), and Theorem 3 (efficient O(|V|) gradient computation) are technically sound
Comprehensive experimental evaluation: Multiple teacher-student pairs, diverse tasks, 10+ baselines, multiple metrics, proper ablations, and reproducible code
Practical efficiency: Elegant factorized decomposition enables linear-time gradient computation despite quadratic objective
Flexible framework: Unified design space with different weighting instantiations for mode-seeking and mode-covering variants
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: Core contribution is adapting Meng et al. (2022) score-matching with log stabilization (straightforward) and factorized weighting. Lou et al. (2024) already applied concrete scores to LMs. Incremental over prior work.

Marginal empirical improvements: ~0.6-3% gains over baselines in most settings; many comparisons within standard deviation bounds (e.g., 24.94±0.29 vs 24.53±0.21). Improvements not commensurate with added complexity.

Unrealistic theoretical assumptions: Propositions 1-2 assume infinite model capacity (|Θ|→∞); unclear whether broader solution set advantage manifests under finite capacity. Theory-practice gap unaddressed.

Restrictive design with limited guidance: Factorization w(y_t,x)=w₁(y_t)w₂(x) prevents joint modeling. Table 5 shows no universal best weighting—(S,S) for generation, (T,S) for calibration. Practitioners lack principled selection strategy. Section D.2 suggests adaptive weighting sometimes necessary, adding complexity.

Insufficient problem characterization: Limited analysis of when logit shift invariance vs. softmax smoothing is actually the bottleneck. Table 3 shows complete collapse of some baselines (0.00 accuracy), suggesting regularization rather than loss function is the real issue.

Presentation issues: Connection between logit shift invariance and concrete score matching solution is indirect. Why relative logits specifically solve shift invariance? Large paper (34pp) with dense presentation; key insights could be more prominent.

Missing practical guidance: No systematic sensitivity analysis for w₁, w₂. No clear characterization of when to prefer CSD over DLD/KL. No failure mode analysis. Table 9 shows computation nearly identical to baselines, questioning efficiency gains.

Limited novelty in design space: Claims to 'open a design space' but only two factorized weighting choices thoroughly explored. Monte Carlo variant for joint weighting acknowledged but dismissed as slower.

strengths: Well-motivated problem with clear identification of softmax-induced smoothing and DLD's solution space restrictions via compelling visualizations
Solid theoretical contributions: Proposition 1 (consistency), Theorem 2 (solution superset), Theorem 3 (O(|V|) gradient efficiency)

Comprehensive experimental validation across diverse settings (task-agnostic, task-specific, chat), multiple architectures (GPT-2, OpenLLaMA, Gemma, Qwen2.5, Gemma2), and 10+ baselines with proper error bars
Flexible framework offering fidelity-diversity trade-offs through weighting design space (S,S), (U,S), (T,S) with principled justification
Practical efficiency achieving O(|V|) gradient computation despite O(|V|²) loss through elegant weight factorization
Strong reproducibility: detailed algorithms, code snippets, extensive appendices, multiple random seeds
weaknesses: Limited fundamental novelty: adapts existing concrete score matching (Meng et al., 2022) with straightforward logarithmic transformation for stability (following Higuchi & Suzuki, 2025)

Significant theory-practice gap: Proposition 1 assumes infinite model capacity (|Θ|→∞); no finite-capacity analysis, sample complexity bounds, or characterization of when the broader solution set provides practical benefits
Modest empirical improvements: ~3% relative gain over SRKL baseline (20.65 vs 20.00, Table 1); improvements often within error margins without significance testing
Weighting function design lacks justification: default w₁=w₂ appears ad-hoc; restrictive factorization constraint; limited practical guidance for choosing weights on new tasks

Concerning edge cases: Task-specific experiments show complete failure modes (0% accuracy, Table 10) for several methods including DLD, suggesting potential instability or implementation issues not adequately investigated
Incomplete analysis of failure modes: cases where DLD-max or DistiLLM-2 outperform CSD not discussed; unclear conditions for when broader solution set actually matters

Presentation issues: critical details scattered across lengthy appendices; logit shift invariance motivation not clearly connected to practical benefits until results; gradient analysis could be deeper
Missing comparisons: DPKD and DistiLLM-2 excluded from main instruction-following experiments; recent direct preference distillation methods not compared
